simonmarais-2017-a1.title: An explicit winning strategy
simonmarais-2017-a1.body:
**Answer: the first player can force a win.**

Only the combinatorics matters: the ten segments are the $10$ pairs of vertices $P_1,\dots,P_5$, and a triangle is any set of three pairs $P_iP_j, P_jP_k, P_kP_i$. So the game is played on the complete graph $K_5$, and **every** permutation of the five vertices is a symmetry of the game (not only the rotations and reflections of the pentagon).

The first player (Blue) starts with $P_1P_2$. Permutations of the vertices fixing the pair $\{P_1,P_2\}$ can move any segment sharing a vertex with $P_1P_2$ to any other such segment, and any segment disjoint from $P_1P_2$ to any other such segment. So we may assume Red replies with $P_2P_3$ (touching $P_1P_2$) or $P_3P_4$ (disjoint from it).

**Case 1: Red plays $P_2P_3$.**
* Blue plays $P_2P_4$. Now Blue threatens $P_1P_4$, which would complete the blue triangle $P_1P_2P_4$. Red has only one segment, so Red cannot win on this move and must block by colouring $P_1P_4$.
* Blue plays $P_2P_5$. Now Blue has **two** threats: $P_1P_5$ (triangle $P_1P_2P_5$) and $P_4P_5$ (triangle $P_2P_4P_5$).
* Red's segments $P_2P_3$ and $P_1P_4$ have no common vertex, so after one more red move Red still has no triangle (a triangle needs three segments that pairwise share a vertex). Red can block only one threat, and Blue completes the other.

**Case 2: Red plays $P_3P_4$.**
* Blue plays $P_1P_5$, threatening $P_2P_5$ (triangle $P_1P_2P_5$). Red cannot win yet, so Red must colour $P_2P_5$.
* Blue plays $P_1P_3$, creating two threats: $P_2P_3$ (triangle $P_1P_2P_3$) and $P_3P_5$ (triangle $P_1P_3P_5$).
* Red's segments $P_3P_4$ and $P_2P_5$ are disjoint, so Red cannot complete a triangle on the next move. Red blocks at most one threat, and Blue wins with the other.

In every case Blue wins by its fourth move, so **the first player can force a win**. ∎

(An exhaustive computer search of the whole game tree confirms this.)

simonmarais-2017-a2.title: The series must diverge
simonmarais-2017-a2.body:
**Answer: yes.** We show that $\sum a_m$ diverges, so its partial sums exceed every bound, in particular $2017^{2017}$.

All terms are positive, and for $m\ge2$ the denominator is at least $a_1^2=1$, so $0<a_m\le 1$ for every $m$. Hence $a_m^2\le a_m$.

* If $a_m\not\to0$, then infinitely many terms are at least some fixed $\varepsilon>0$, and the series of positive terms diverges.
* If $a_m\to0$, then $\dfrac1{a_m}=a_1^2+\cdots+a_{m-1}^2\to\infty$. Using $a_i^2\le a_i$,
$$a_1+a_2+\cdots+a_{m-1}\ \ge\ a_1^2+\cdots+a_{m-1}^2=\frac1{a_m}\longrightarrow\infty .$$

In both cases the partial sums are unbounded, so some $N$ has $a_1+\cdots+a_N>2017^{2017}$. ∎

simonmarais-2017-a2.title: Estimate the growth
simonmarais-2017-a2.body:
**Answer: yes.**

Let $Q_m=a_1^2+\cdots+a_m^2$, so $Q_1=1$, $a_{m+1}=1/Q_m$ and
$$Q_{m+1}=Q_m+\frac1{Q_m^2}.$$
Since $Q_m\ge1$,
$$Q_{m+1}^3=Q_m^3+3+\frac{3}{Q_m^3}+\frac1{Q_m^6}\le Q_m^3+7 ,$$
so by induction $Q_m^3\le 7m-6\le 7m$. Therefore
$$a_{m+1}=\frac1{Q_m}\ge (7m)^{-1/3}.$$
For any $M$,
$$a_2+\cdots+a_{M+1}\ \ge\ \sum_{m=1}^{M}(7m)^{-1/3}\ \ge\ M\cdot(7M)^{-1/3}=\frac{M^{2/3}}{7^{1/3}},$$
which tends to infinity. (In fact $Q_m^3\sim 3m$, so the partial sums grow like a constant times $N^{2/3}$.) Hence a suitable $N$ exists. ∎

simonmarais-2017-a3.title: Row operations with inclusion–exclusion
simonmarais-2017-a3.body:
Write $N=n+1\ge2$. For a positive integer $m$ let $v(m)\in\mathbb R^n$ be the vector whose $j$-th coordinate is $1$ if $j\mid m$ and $0$ otherwise. The rows of $M(n)$ are $v(2),v(3),\dots,v(N)$, and $v(1)=(1,0,\dots,0)$.

Let $N=p_1^{a_1}\cdots p_k^{a_k}$ ($k\ge1$, distinct primes, $a_i\ge1$), and for $I\subseteq\{1,\dots,k\}$ put $p_I=\prod_{i\in I}p_i$.

**Lemma.** $\displaystyle\sum_{I\subseteq\{1,\dots,k\}}(-1)^{|I|}\,v\!\left(\frac{N}{p_I}\right)=0.$

*Proof.* Fix a coordinate $j\in\{1,\dots,n\}$. If $j\nmid N$, then $j$ divides none of the numbers $N/p_I$, so every summand has $j$-th coordinate $0$. If $j\mid N$, write $N/j=\prod p_i^{b_i}$ and $J=\{i:b_i\ge1\}$. Then $j\mid N/p_I \iff p_I\mid N/j\iff I\subseteq J$, so the $j$-th coordinate of the sum is $\sum_{I\subseteq J}(-1)^{|I|}$. Since $j\le n<N$, we have $N/j>1$, so $J\ne\varnothing$ and this alternating sum is $(1-1)^{|J|}=0$. $\square$

The numbers $N/p_I$ are distinct divisors of $N$; the one with $I=\varnothing$ is $N$ itself (the last row), all others are smaller than $N$.

**$N$ not square-free $\Rightarrow$ $M(n)$ singular.** Some $a_i\ge2$, so even $N/p_{\{1,\dots,k\}}=\prod p_i^{a_i-1}$ is at least $2$. Hence for every $I\neq\varnothing$, $2\le N/p_I\le n$, i.e. $v(N/p_I)$ is a row of $M(n)$ other than the last. The Lemma expresses the last row $v(N)$ as a linear combination of other rows, so $\det M(n)=0$.

**$N$ square-free $\Rightarrow$ $M(n)$ invertible.** Now $N=p_1\cdots p_k$ and $N/p_I=1$ exactly for $I=\{1,\dots,k\}$. For $I\neq\varnothing,\{1,\dots,k\}$ the vectors $v(N/p_I)$ are rows of $M(n)$ other than the last, so adding suitable multiples of them to the last row (which does not change the determinant) replaces $v(N)$ by
$$\sum_{I\ne\{1,\dots,k\}}(-1)^{|I|}v\!\left(\tfrac N{p_I}\right)=-(-1)^k v(1)=\pm(1,0,\dots,0),$$
by the Lemma. Expanding along this new last row, $\det M(n)=\pm\det M'$, where $M'$ is obtained by deleting the last row and the first column. Index the rows of $M'$ by $r=i+1\in\{2,\dots,n\}$ and the columns by $c=j\in\{2,\dots,n\}$; the entry is $1$ iff $c\mid r$. This is $0$ for $c>r$ and $1$ for $c=r$, so $M'$ is lower triangular with $1$s on the diagonal and $\det M'=1$. (For $n=1$, $M(1)=(1)$ directly.) Thus $\det M(n)=\pm1\neq0$.

Hence $M(n)$ is invertible if and only if $n+1$ is square-free. ∎

simonmarais-2017-a3.title: Möbius inversion and a cofactor
simonmarais-2017-a3.body:
Let $D$ be the $(n+1)\times(n+1)$ matrix with $D_{ij}=1$ if $j\mid i$ and $0$ otherwise ($1\le i,j\le n+1$). It is lower triangular with $1$s on the diagonal, so $\det D=1$. Deleting **row $1$ and column $n+1$** of $D$ leaves exactly $M(n)$ (row $i+1$ of $D$ is row $i$ of $M(n)$).

**Inverse of $D$.** Let $E_{jk}=\mu(j/k)$ if $k\mid j$ and $0$ otherwise, where $\mu$ is the Möbius function. Then
$$(DE)_{ik}=\sum_{k\mid j\mid i}\mu(j/k)=\sum_{d\mid i/k}\mu(d)=\begin{cases}1,&i=k\\0,&i\ne k\end{cases}$$
when $k\mid i$ (and $(DE)_{ik}=0$ when $k\nmid i$), using $\sum_{d\mid m}\mu(d)=[m=1]$. So $D^{-1}=E$.

**Cofactor formula.** Since $D^{-1}=\operatorname{adj}(D)/\det D=\operatorname{adj}(D)$,
$$(D^{-1})_{n+1,1}=C_{1,n+1}=(-1)^{1+(n+1)}\det M(n),$$
where $C_{1,n+1}$ is the cofactor of entry $(1,n+1)$ of $D$. But $(D^{-1})_{n+1,1}=E_{n+1,1}=\mu(n+1)$. Hence
$$\det M(n)=(-1)^n\,\mu(n+1).$$
Since $\mu(n+1)\ne0$ exactly when $n+1$ is square-free (and then $\mu(n+1)=\pm1$), $M(n)$ is invertible if and only if $n+1$ is square-free. ∎

simonmarais-2017-a4.title: The vector is a gradient — minimise
simonmarais-2017-a4.body:
**A potential.** For a fixed point $A=(a,b)$ and $P=(x,y)\ne A$,
$$\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\frac1{\|PA\|^3}=\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\big[(x-a)^2+(y-b)^2\big]^{-3/2}=\frac{3(a-x)}{\|PA\|^5},$$
and similarly for $y$. Since $\overrightarrow{PA}=(a-x,b-y)$, the gradient of $P\mapsto \|PA\|^{-3}$ is $3\,\overrightarrow{PA}/\|PA\|^5$. Hence for
$$f(P)=\sum_{k=1}^{2017}\frac{k}{\|PA_k\|^3}\qquad(P\notin\{A_1,\dots,A_{2017}\})$$
we get $\nabla f(P)=3\sum_k k\,\overrightarrow{PA_k}/\|PA_k\|^5$. So it suffices to find a point where $\nabla f=0$, e.g. a local minimum of $f$.

**Setting.** Place the polygon in the unit circle centred at the origin $O$, and let $D$ be the closed unit disc. Then
$$f(O)=\sum_{k=1}^{2017}k=\frac{2017\cdot2018}2=2\,035\,153 .$$

**$f$ is large on the circle.** The vertices cut the circle into arcs of length $2\pi/2017$, so every point $Q$ of the circle is within arc length $\pi/2017$ of some vertex $A_j$, and the straight distance is at most the arc length. If $Q$ is not a vertex,
$$f(Q)\ \ge\ \frac{j}{\|QA_j\|^3}\ \ge\ \Big(\frac{2017}{\pi}\Big)^3>\Big(\frac{2017}{4}\Big)^3>10^8>f(O).$$

**$f$ is large near the vertices.** Let $r=1/200$. If $\|PA_j\|<r$ then $f(P)\ge 1/r^3=8\cdot10^6>f(O)$.

**A minimum exists and is a critical point.** Let $K$ be $D$ with the open discs of radius $r$ about the vertices removed. $K$ is compact, contains $O$, and $f$ is continuous on $K$, so $f$ attains a minimum on $K$ at some $P^*$, with $f(P^*)\le f(O)$. Every point of $D\setminus K$ (other than vertices) has $f>f(O)$, so $P^*$ minimises $f$ over all of $D\setminus\{A_1,\dots,A_{2017}\}$. Moreover $P^*$ is not on the unit circle and not on the boundary of any removed disc (there $f>f(O)\ge f(P^*)$), so $P^*$ is an interior point of $K$. Thus $P^*$ is a local minimum of the differentiable function $f$, and $\nabla f(P^*)=0$.

Therefore $P=P^*$ satisfies $\sum_k k\,\overrightarrow{PA_k}/\|PA_k\|^5=\tfrac13\nabla f(P^*)=\vec 0$. ∎

simonmarais-2017-b1.title: Solve the linear system
simonmarais-2017-b1.body:
Let the vertices be $1,2,3,4$ and write $e_{ij}$ for the length of edge $ij$. The labels are
$$S_1=e_{12}+e_{13}+e_{14},\quad S_2=e_{12}+e_{23}+e_{24},\quad S_3=e_{13}+e_{23}+e_{34},\quad S_4=e_{14}+e_{24}+e_{34}.$$

**Opposite edges are equal.** Since all labels are equal,
$$0=S_1+S_2-S_3-S_4=2e_{12}-2e_{34},$$
so $e_{12}=e_{34}$. In the same way $S_1+S_3-S_2-S_4=2e_{13}-2e_{24}=0$ and $S_1+S_4-S_2-S_3=2e_{14}-2e_{23}=0$. Put
$$a=e_{12}=e_{34},\qquad b=e_{13}=e_{24},\qquad c=e_{14}=e_{23}.$$

**Conclusion.** The edges at vertex $1$ have lengths $e_{12},e_{13},e_{14}=a,b,c$; at vertex $2$: $e_{12},e_{24},e_{23}=a,b,c$; at vertex $3$: $e_{13},e_{34},e_{23}=b,a,c$; at vertex $4$: $e_{14},e_{24},e_{34}=c,b,a$. On the other hand, the face $123$ has sides $e_{12},e_{23},e_{13}=a,c,b$. A face of a (non-degenerate) tetrahedron is a genuine triangle, so $a,b,c$ satisfy the strict triangle inequalities. Hence at every vertex the three edge lengths are the side lengths of a triangle (namely of any face). ∎

simonmarais-2017-b1.title: Subtracting pairs of equations
simonmarais-2017-b1.body:
This is the official route. Label the edges $a,b,c,d,e,f$ with $a$ opposite $d$, $b$ opposite $e$, $c$ opposite $f$, arranged so that the four vertex sums are
$$a+b+c=b+d+f=c+d+e=a+e+f .$$
From the first equality, $a+c=d+f$; from the equality of the third and fourth sums, $c+d=a+f$. Adding these gives $a+2c+d=a+d+2f$, so $c=f$. The same argument with the roles of the pairs permuted gives $a=d$ and $b=e$.

So every vertex meets edges of lengths $a,b,c$ (one from each pair of opposite edges), and every face also has side lengths $a,b,c$ (a face contains exactly one edge from each opposite pair). Since a face is a triangle, $a,b,c$ are the sides of a triangle, as required. ∎

simonmarais-2017-b2.title: Parity, then factorise
simonmarais-2017-b2.body:
**Answer: only $(p,q)=(2,2)$**, which works since $2^1+2^1=4=2^2$.

**Both odd is impossible.** If $p,q$ are odd primes, then $q-1$ and $p-1$ are even, so $p^{q-1}$ and $q^{p-1}$ are squares of odd numbers and hence $\equiv1\pmod 4$. Their sum is $\equiv2\pmod4$, but squares are $\equiv0$ or $1\pmod 4$.

**One of them is $2$.** By symmetry let $q=2$; we need $p+2^{p-1}=m^2$ for a positive integer $m$. The case $p=2$ is the solution above, so let $p$ be odd and put $t=\tfrac{p-1}2\ge1$. Then
$$p=m^2-2^{2t}=(m-2^t)(m+2^t).$$
Both factors are integers, the second is positive, so the first is positive too; as $p$ is prime and $m-2^t<m+2^t$, we must have $m-2^t=1$ and $m+2^t=p$. Subtracting, $p=2^{t+1}+1$.

But $2^{s}\ge 2s$ for every integer $s\ge1$ (true for $s=1,2$, and $2^{s+1}=2\cdot2^s\ge4s\ge2(s+1)$), so
$$2^{t+1}+1\ \ge\ 2(t+1)+1=p+2>p,$$
a contradiction. Hence there are no solutions with $p$ odd, and $(2,2)$ is the only pair. ∎

simonmarais-2017-b2.title: Bounding $p$ instead (official route)
simonmarais-2017-b2.body:
As in the first approach, if both primes are odd the sum is $\equiv 2 \pmod 4$, which is not a square; so we may take $q=2$ and $p$ odd with $p+2^{p-1}=m^2$, giving
$$\big(m-2^{(p-1)/2}\big)\big(m+2^{(p-1)/2}\big)=p .$$
So $p$ equals the larger factor: $p=m+2^{(p-1)/2}>2^{(p-1)/2}$.

**Claim:** $n<2^{(n-1)/2}$ for all integers $n\ge7$. For $n=7$: $7<8$. If $n<2^{(n-1)/2}$ for some $n\ge7$, then
$$n+1=\frac{n+1}{n}\cdot n<\frac87\cdot 2^{(n-1)/2}<\sqrt2\cdot 2^{(n-1)/2}=2^{n/2},$$
since $\frac87<\sqrt2$. This proves the claim.

So only $p=3$ and $p=5$ remain: $3+2^2=7$ and $5+2^4=21$ are not squares. Hence $(p,q)=(2,2)$ is the only solution. ∎

simonmarais-2017-b3.title: Connectivity and a minimal path
simonmarais-2017-b3.body:
Throughout, "point" means lattice point. Two observations used repeatedly:

* **(R)** If $X$ is blue and $R$ is red, then $2X-R$ is blue (otherwise $X$, the midpoint of the red points $R$ and $2X-R$, would be a blue point on a red segment).
* **(N)** Two lattice points at distance $2$ differ by $(\pm2,0)$ or $(0,\pm2)$. So the second rule says: if $R$ is red, then for each axis direction $e$, at least one of $R+e$, $R-e$ is red.
* All conditions are invariant under translations by lattice vectors, the reflections $x\mapsto -x$, $y\mapsto-y$, and swapping the coordinates.

Call two red points *adjacent* if they are at distance $1$; this makes the red points into a graph.

**Lemma 1. The red graph is connected.** Suppose not, and pick red $A,B$ in different components with $|AB|$ minimal; then $|AB|>1$. If a red point $C$ had $|AC|<|AB|$ and $|BC|<|AB|$, then $C$ would lie in a different component from $A$ or from $B$, contradicting minimality. Every lattice point inside segment $AB$ is red (first rule) and would be such a $C$, so $AB$ contains no lattice points other than $A,B$. In particular $A,B$ differ in both coordinates (otherwise $|AB|=1$), and by symmetry $B-A=(p,q)$ with $p,q\ge1$. The point $A+(1,0)$ has distance $1<|AB|$ to $A$ and $\sqrt{(p-1)^2+q^2}<|AB|$ to $B$, so it is blue; by (N), $A-(1,0)$ is red. Likewise $B-(0,1)$ is blue and $B+(0,1)$ is red. Now take $A_0\in\{A,A-(1,0)\}$ and $B_0\in\{B,B+(0,1)\}$ so that $A_0+B_0$ has both coordinates even (the four choices realise all four parity classes of $A_0+B_0$). Then $C=(A_0+B_0)/2$ is a lattice point on a red segment, hence red, and
$$C-A=\Big(\tfrac{p-\delta}{2},\tfrac{q+\varepsilon}{2}\Big),\quad C-B=\Big(\tfrac{-p-\delta}{2},\tfrac{-q+\varepsilon}{2}\Big),\qquad \delta,\varepsilon\in\{0,1\}.$$
So $|AC|^2\le\frac{p^2+(q+1)^2}{4}<p^2+q^2$ and $|BC|^2\le\frac{(p+1)^2+q^2}4<p^2+q^2$, a contradiction. $\square$

**Two geometric facts.** (F1) For any four points $Z,P,Q,R$, triangle $PQR\subseteq ZPQ\cup ZQR\cup ZRP$: for $Y\in PQR$, $Y\neq Z$, the ray from $Z$ through $Y$ leaves the triangle $PQR$ at a boundary point $W$ beyond (or at) $Y$; $W$ lies on a side, say $QR$, and then $Y\in ZW\subseteq ZQR$. (F2) The convex hull of a finite set $M$ is the union of the triangles with vertices in $M$. Also, a blue point lying in a triangle with red vertices is never on its sides (first rule), so it lies in the **interior**.

**Setting up a minimal counterexample.** Suppose red $A,B,C$ have a blue point in the interior of triangle $ABC$. By Lemma 1, $A,B,C$ lie in a finite connected set of red points. Among all finite connected sets $S$ of red points whose convex hull contains a blue point, choose one with $|S|$ minimal. By (F2), some triangle with vertices in $S$ contains a blue point (in its interior).

**Lemma 2.** If $P\in S$ and $S\setminus\{P\}$ is connected, then every triangle with vertices in $S$ containing a blue point has $P$ as a vertex. (Otherwise $S\setminus\{P\}$ would be a smaller valid set.)

**Lemma 3.** $S$ is an induced path $R_1R_2\cdots R_n$ ($R_i$ adjacent to $R_j$ iff $|i-j|=1$). *Proof.* Call $P$ *removable* if $S\setminus\{P\}$ is connected; endpoints of a spanning tree are removable. If $S$ is not an induced path, it has three removable points $P_1,P_2,P_3$. (Take a spanning tree; if it has $\ge3$ leaves we are done. Otherwise it is a path $R_1\cdots R_n$ with an extra edge $R_iR_j$, $i<j-1$. If $R_iR_j=R_1R_n$, the graph contains a cycle through all points and every point is removable. If $i>1$, replacing the edge $R_{j-1}R_j$ by $R_iR_j$ gives a spanning tree with leaves $R_1,R_{j-1},R_n$; if $i=1<j<n$, replacing $R_1R_2$ by $R_1R_j$ gives leaves $R_1,R_2,R_n$.) By Lemma 2 the only triangle in $S$ that can contain a blue point is $P_1P_2P_3$. If $S=\{P_1,P_2,P_3\}$, these are three unit-connected lattice points, and such a triangle has no interior lattice points — contradiction. Otherwise take another $Z\in S$: by (F1) the blue point in $P_1P_2P_3$ lies in one of $ZP_1P_2,ZP_2P_3,ZP_3P_1$, each missing some $P_i$, contradicting Lemma 2. $\square$

**The final contradiction.** Since $R_1$ and $R_n$ are removable, by Lemma 2 every blue point of the hull lies inside a triangle $R_1R_jR_n$ with $1<j<n$. Among the finitely many blue points in the hull of $S$, choose $B$ maximising the area of triangle $R_1BR_n$; by symmetry (relabel the path backwards) assume $|R_1B|\ge|R_nB|$. Let $B$ lie inside $R_1R_jR_n$. By (F1) with $Z=R_2$, $B$ lies in $R_1R_2R_j$, $R_2R_jR_n$ or $R_1R_2R_n$; the first two miss $R_n$ or $R_1$, so by Lemma 2, $B$ is in the interior of $R_1R_2R_n$.

Let $X=2B-R_n$; it is blue by (R), and $\operatorname{area}(XR_1R_n)=2\operatorname{area}(BR_1R_n)>0$, so by maximality $X$ lies outside the hull of $S$, in particular outside triangle $R_1R_2R_n$. The ray from $R_n$ through the interior point $B$ leaves this triangle through the open side $R_1R_2$, before reaching $X$. So the segments $R_nX$ and $R_1R_2$ cross at interior points, and $R_1XR_2R_n$ is a convex quadrilateral (all interior angles $<180^\circ$).

* Let $M$ be the midpoint of $R_1R_n$. As $|R_1B|\ge|R_nB|$, $B$ lies on $R_n$'s side of the perpendicular bisector of $R_1R_n$ (or on it), so $\angle R_nMB\le90^\circ$. The homothety with centre $R_n$ and ratio $2$ maps $M\mapsto R_1$, $B\mapsto X$, so $\angle R_nR_1X=\angle R_nMB\le90^\circ$.
* In the convex quadrilateral the diagonal $R_1R_2$ splits this angle, so $\angle R_2R_1R_n<90^\circ$ and $\angle R_2R_1X<90^\circ$.
* **Lattice fact:** if $U,V,W$ are lattice points, $|UV|=1$ and $\angle VUW<90^\circ$ with $W$ not on line $UV$, then $\angle UWV\le45^\circ$. Indeed, after a symmetry $U=(0,0)$, $V=(1,0)$, $W=(a,b)$ with $b\ge1$, and $\angle VUW<90^\circ$ means $a\ge1$. With $u=U-W$, $v=V-W$: $u\cdot v=a(a-1)+b^2\ge b^2>0$ and $|u\times v|=b$, so $\tan\angle UWV=\frac{b}{a(a-1)+b^2}\le\frac1b\le1$.
* Applying this with $U=R_1$, $V=R_2$: $\angle R_1R_nR_2\le45^\circ$ and $\angle R_1XR_2\le45^\circ$.

The angles of $R_1XR_2R_n$ sum to $360^\circ$, so $\angle XR_2R_n\ge360^\circ-90^\circ-45^\circ-45^\circ=180^\circ$, contradicting convexity.

Therefore no triangle with red vertices contains a blue point in its interior. ∎

simonmarais-2017-b4.title: What is known
simonmarais-2017-b4.body:
**This is an open research problem; no complete answer is known.** The competition awarded points for partial progress (non-trivial bounds).

**Reformulation.** The tiles are rhombi with unit sides, and $C(n)$ counts the rhombus tilings of the regular $2n$-gon. These are in bijection with many other objects, for example:
* commutation classes of reduced words of the longest element of the symmetric group $S_n$;
* primitive sorting networks on $n$ elements;
* simple arrangements of $n$ pseudolines (equivalently, uniform oriented matroids of rank $3$ on $n$ elements).

This is sequence A006245 in the OEIS, first studied by D. E. Knuth (*Axioms and Hulls*, 1992). Its first values, starting from $C(1)=1$, are
$$1,\ 1,\ 2,\ 8,\ 62,\ 908,\ 24698,\ 1232944,\ 112018190,\ 18410581880,\ \dots$$
For instance $C(2)=1$ (the square is a single tile) and $C(3)=2$ (a regular hexagon can be split into three rhombi in two ways).

**Bounds.** Counting arguments for pseudoline arrangements show that $\log_2 C(n)$ grows like a constant times $n^2$. The best bounds quoted in the official solutions are those of S. Felsner and P. Valtr (*Coding and counting arrangements of pseudolines*): for all sufficiently large $n$,
$$2^{0.1887\,n^2}\le C(n)\le 2^{0.6571\,n^2},$$
so
$$0.1887\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log_2 C(n)}{n^2}\le\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log_2 C(n)}{n^2}\le0.6571 .$$
Whether the limit exists, and what its value is, is unknown.
